Gold Ridge Meyer Lemon Olive Oil

blocks.c: Gold Ridge Meyer Lemon Olive Oil

blocks.x: Spend any time in Northern California and you’ll find it credibly doubles for the Mediterranean, with white fields of sun-bleached grasses that contrast sharply with the lush emerald of vineyards. And beside them, so, so many olive groves. This past summer I was lucky to visit Gold Ridge Organic Farms in Sebastopol, which cultivates, among other things, a range of different Mediterranean olives including the Frantoio, Arbequina, and Picholine varieties. I was particularly moved by its Meyer Lemon Olive Oil, which delivers a bright aroma and fragrant citrus on the palate that uplifts the gently bitter spice of the oil. The olives are co-milled with Meyer lemons, also grown on-site, so the final product is actually citrus-flavored—no chemicals involved. I like it as a finishing oil or in salad dressings, which keeps as much of the fruit’s delicate flavor and aromas intact as possible. I'm apparently not this product's only fan—lauded fine dining spot Lazy Bear in San Francisco is a long-time buyer of Gold Ridge's Meyer lemon and other oils. —Rachel Tepper Paley, site director
Dieux x Fishwife Glowing Skin Bundle

blocks.c: Dieux x Fishwife Glowing Skin Bundle

blocks.x: The first time I saw that Fishwife, the beloved tinned fish brand with the best packaging in the game, was making eye patches (the kind you put under your eyes for brightening and hydrating), I did a double take. But Fishwife teamed up with Dieux, a skincare brand known for its reusable silicone eye masks, to make skincare you can wear to pair with skincare you can eat (aka the brand’s sardines with preserved lemons, packed with Omega-3s). As you’d expect from Fishwife, the design on the patches is incredibly cute. Eating sardines straight out of the tin while wearing the patches in the comfort of my own home is my kind of self-care. You can buy the patches on their own or else a bundle complete with sardines too. And don’t worry: there is no actual tinned fish in the eye patches. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager
